title: Practice designs in order: link shortener, rate limiter, chat, feed, retrieval service, agent platform
story:
This track has covered every component separately, and knowing them separately is not the same as being able to assemble one under questioning. The six designs below are ordered so that each adds exactly one new constraint over the last, which means what you are practising is assembly rather than recall.

The link shortener comes first because it is the simplest system that is not trivial. It establishes the shape: generate an identifier, store a mapping, read it back far more often than you wrote it. The constraint it introduces is the read-write ratio, and everything about the design follows from it — this is a caching problem wearing a storage costume. The estimation figures decide the argument: a main memory reference is around a hundred nanoseconds against a disk seek at around ten million, so whether the working set fits in memory is the whole question.

A rate limiter adds shared state on the hot path. Now every request must consult and update something common, which is the serial fraction the scaling lesson warned about, and the design turns on where that state lives. Count per machine and your real limit is the stated one multiplied by the fleet. Count centrally and you have put a dependency in the place you can least afford one.

A chat system adds delivery and ordering. Messages must reach recipients who may be offline, and two messages sent at nearly the same moment need an order that everyone agrees on — which the concurrency lesson says does not exist for free, because there is no shared now. The ordering you present is a convention you chose.

A feed adds fan-out, and with it the arithmetic that makes this the hardest of the six. A request that depends on many components inherits their worst case rather than their average: with a single server at a ninety-ninth percentile of one second, a fan-out to a hundred servers sees a slow response more often than not, and at two thousand servers even a one in ten thousand chance means eighteen percent of requests exceed a second. Fan-out on write or fan-out on read is the real decision, and the celebrity account is the hot key problem arriving in person.

A retrieval service adds a quality dimension that none of the previous four have. Those either return the right answer or fail visibly. This one can return something plausible and wrong, silently, because retrieval always returns its nearest candidates whether or not anything relevant exists. So the design must include how you measure whether it worked, which is a component the earlier designs did not need.

An agent platform adds dependent steps, and everything compounds. Cost, latency and the probability of at least one error all multiply with loop length rather than adding, and an early mistake becomes a later premise rather than an outlier. It also inherits every constraint above it: serving needs batching, and batch size is limited by per-request cache memory that is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically.

Work them in order. And the value is in being interrupted — practising a sequence produces fluency in that sequence, so ask somebody to change the scale halfway through, or to remove the assumption you leaned on.

problem.name: Assembly under questioning
problem.shape: The components are known individually and have never been assembled into a whole while somebody is asking why.
tell: you can explain each component and stall when asked to combine them
practice consists of reading architectures rather than producing them
every practice run follows the same path to the same answer
no practice design has ever been interrupted
problem.move: Work the six in order, each adding one constraint, and say aloud what each addition forces. Then have the assumptions changed mid-design — the scale raised, the consistency requirement tightened, the hot key introduced — because fluency in an uninterrupted path is not the skill being built.
problem.invariant: Each design in the sequence introduces exactly one new constraint over its predecessor, so a difficulty encountered can be attributed to the constraint that caused it rather than to the design as a whole.
problem.breaks: Practising a fixed sequence produces fluency in that sequence. The ordering that makes each constraint legible also makes the path memorable, so a run that follows it smoothly demonstrates recall of the path rather than the ability to assemble — which is why the interruption is the exercise rather than a complication of it.

cost.time: six designs worked properly, which is hours rather than minutes, and the interruptions make each longer
cost.beats: reading architecture write-ups, which builds recognition rather than production, and practising one design repeatedly, which builds fluency in one shape

worked.problem: Which constraint does each design in the sequence introduce?
worked.reasoning:
Each adds exactly one thing its predecessor did not have, which is the point of the ordering — a difficulty you hit can be attributed to the constraint that caused it.

The link shortener introduces the read-write ratio. Writes are rare, reads are common, and the mapping is small. Everything follows: this is a caching problem, and the deciding question is whether the working set fits in memory, since a memory reference is around a hundred nanoseconds against a disk seek at around ten million. Nothing else about it is hard, which is why it comes first.

The rate limiter introduces shared state on the hot path. Every request must now consult and update something common, which is a serial fraction, and the whole design is about where that state lives. Per machine and your real limit is the stated one multiplied by the fleet size; centrally and you have added a dependency to the path you can least afford one on. There is no free answer, only a choice about which unfairness you accept.

Chat introduces delivery and ordering. Recipients may be offline, so delivery becomes a durability question, and two messages sent at nearly the same moment need an order everyone agrees on — which does not exist for free, because there is no shared now across machines. The ordering you present is a convention you chose rather than a fact you discovered.

The feed introduces fan-out, and it is the hardest of the six because the arithmetic is unforgiving. A request depending on many components inherits their worst case: at a ninety-ninth percentile of one second, fanning out to a hundred servers sees a slow response more often than not, and at two thousand servers even one in ten thousand leaves eighteen percent of requests over a second. The real decision is fan-out on write versus on read, and the celebrity account is the hot key problem arriving in person — one key that no amount of partitioning spreads.

The retrieval service introduces a quality dimension none of the previous four have. Those either return the right answer or fail visibly. This one can return something plausible and wrong, silently, because retrieval always returns its nearest candidates whether or not anything relevant exists. So the design must include how you would know it was working, which is a component the earlier designs did not need at all.

The agent platform introduces dependent steps, and everything compounds — cost, latency and the probability of at least one error multiply with loop length rather than adding, and an early error becomes a later premise rather than an outlier to discard. It also inherits every constraint above it, including that serving needs batching and batch size is limited by per-request cache memory that is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically.

The thing I would add is about how to practise rather than what. Working the sequence smoothly demonstrates fluency in the sequence, which is not the skill. The value is in being interrupted — having the scale raised by two orders of magnitude, the consistency requirement tightened, or the assumption you leaned on removed — because that is what actually happens, and recovering from it is the thing being built.

problem.practice: Work all six in order, aloud, writing assumptions as you go. Then do the feed again with someone raising the scale by two orders of magnitude halfway through, and notice which of your earlier decisions had to be undone.
